id: A Note Left in Jimmy Leonard’s Shack

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Near the dry river’s water-mark we found Your brother Minnegan, Flopped like a fish against the muddy ground. Beany, the kid whose yellow hair turns green, Told me to find you, even in the rain, And tell you he was drowned. I hid behind the chassis on the bank, The wreck of someone’s Ford: I was afraid to come and wake you drunk: You told me once the waking up was hard, The daylight beating at you like a board. Blood in my stomach sank. Beside, you told him never to go out Along the river-side Drinking and singing, clattering about. You might have thrown a rock at me and cried I was to blame, I let him fall in the road And pitch down on his side. Well, I’ll get hell enough when I get home For coming up this far, Leaving the note, and running as I came. I’ll go and tell my father where you are. You’d better go find Minnegan before Policemen hear and come. Beany went home, and I got sick and ran, You old son of a bitch. You better hurry down to Minnegan; He’s drunk or dying now, I don’t know which, Rolled in the roots and garbage like a fish, The poor old man.

outputs.L1:
Near the dry river’s waterline, we found  
Your brother Minnegan, flopping like a fish  
Against the muddy ground. Beany—the kid  
Whose yellow hair turns green—told me to find you,  
Even in the rain, and tell you he had drowned.

I hid behind the chassis on the bank,  
The wreckage of someone’s Ford. I was afraid  
To come and wake you, drunk. You once told me  
How hard the waking was, the daylight beating  
Against you like a board. The blood sank  
In my stomach.

Besides, you had warned him never to go out  
Along the riverside, drinking and singing,  
Clattering about. You might have thrown  
A rock at me and cried that I was to blame—  
That I had let him fall into the road  
And pitch down on his side.

Well, I’ll catch hell enough when I get home  
For coming up this far, leaving the note,  
And running as I came. I’ll go and tell  
My father where you are.

You’d better find Minnegan before  
The policemen hear and come. Beany went home,  
And I got sick and ran, you old son of a bitch.

You’d better hurry down to Minnegan.  
He’s drunk or dying now—I don’t know which—  
Rolled among the roots and garbage like a fish,  
The poor old man.
outputs.L2:
Down by the dry riverbed, close to the old high-water line,  
we came upon your brother, Minnegan,  
sprawled on the mud and thrashing like a stranded fish.  

Beany—the boy with yellow hair that takes on a greenish tint—  
sent me through the rain to look for you  
and say that Minnegan had drowned.  

I crouched out of sight behind the frame  
of somebody’s wrecked Ford on the bank.  
I was scared to approach and rouse you from your drunken sleep.  
You once said coming awake was painful,  
that daylight struck you with the force of a plank.  
My insides went cold with fear.  

And you had warned him not to wander  
beside the river,  
boozing, singing, and making a racket.  
I thought you might hurl a stone at me  
and shout that it was my fault—  
that I had allowed him to collapse in the road  
and tumble onto his side.  

I’ll be punished badly enough when I return home  
for traveling all this way,  
leaving only a message, and then fleeing as I arrived.  
I’m going to tell my father where you can be found.  

You should reach Minnegan before the police  
learn what happened and show up.  
Beany has already gone home. I became sick and ran,  
you miserable old bastard.  

Get down to Minnegan quickly.  
I can’t tell whether he is merely drunk or close to death.  
He lies curled among roots and refuse, flopping like a fish—  
the unfortunate old man.
outputs.L3:
The speaker finds Minnegan lying near the muddy riverbank, unsure whether he has drowned, passed out from drinking, or is close to death. Alarmed by the discovery, Beany sends the frightened speaker to find Minnegan’s brother and tell him what has happened.

The speaker is reluctant to wake the brother because he is drunk and may respond violently or blame the messenger for Minnegan’s condition. After all, Minnegan had already been warned not to wander along the riverside while drinking and singing. Nevertheless, the situation is urgent. The speaker urges the brother to reach Minnegan before the police arrive and then plans to inform their father as well.
outputs.L4:
The child burst through the doorway, panting so hard that for several seconds no words came. His face was white beneath streaks of dirt, and his hands trembled at his sides.

“Come quick,” he said at last. “Please, you’ve got to come quick. It’s Minnegan—he’s down by the river.”

The man at the table barely lifted his head. An empty bottle lay on its side beside him, and another stood between his loose, unsteady fingers. His eyes were swollen and unfocused.

“What are you shouting about?” he muttered.

“I found him,” the child rushed on. “I didn’t mean to leave him there. I tried to pull him up, but the bank was slippery, and he was so heavy. There was mud all over his clothes, and his face was in the water at first. I turned him over—I did, I swear—but he wouldn’t wake up.”

The man stared at him without seeming to understand.

“He’s by the old landing,” the child continued, choking on every breath. “Where people throw the broken boxes and bottles. There’s rubbish caught in the reeds, and the water smells bad. Minnegan’s lying right in it. One of his shoes is gone. I called his name over and over, but he didn’t answer. Maybe he breathed once. I don’t know. I was scared.”

He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand.

“I should’ve stayed with him. I know I should have, but it was getting dark, and the river kept moving him a little every time the water came up. I thought he might slide back in. I tried to hold him, but then I thought you’d know what to do. You’re his brother. You have to come.”

At that, the man’s fingers tightened around the bottle. For an instant, something like fear broke through the fog in his eyes. He pushed himself upright, knocking the chair backward, but staggered and caught the edge of the table.

The child seized his sleeve.

“Please,” he whispered. “Before it’s too late.”

Outside, the river moved silently past the heaps of refuse along its banks. In the mud near the landing, Minnegan lay motionless among rotting boards, torn paper, and shattered glass—abandoned in a place where no one looked closely and no one came quickly. The child pulled the drunken man toward the door, carrying a terror and guilt far too heavy for him, while the man struggled to follow through the ruin his drinking had made of them all.
outputs.L5:
**Near You, Minnegan**

Minnegan had spent years searching for a place that felt like home. He crossed crowded cities, quiet valleys, and windswept shores, believing happiness waited somewhere beyond the horizon.

One evening, he returned to the small town where his journey had begun. A familiar voice called his name, and suddenly he understood: what mattered most had never been far away.

“Home,” his old friend told him, “is wherever the people who love you are near.”

Minnegan smiled. Sometimes, the end of your journey is closer than you think.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bleak dramatic-monologue poem in which a frightened child tells a drunken man that his brother may be dead by the river.
counterfactuals.output:
Don’t sleep, sir. Please. The rain’s come in.  
It’s black along the landing.  
I know you said the river talks  
and no one understands it,

but Jamie went to fetch your coat—  
the good one, from the willow—  
and now the reeds are whispering  
with his cap caught in their shadow.

I called him twice. I called him six.  
The bridge gave back my crying.  
There’s something pale below the bank.  
I think it may be lying.

No, don’t pour more. The bottle won’t  
make morning any nearer.  
You’re bigger than the dark, you said.  
You said the dead don’t hear us.

Please stand. I cannot go alone.  
The mud has filled my slippers.  
The moon keeps breaking on the water  
into little silver splinters.

Perhaps he’s cold. Perhaps he waits.  
Perhaps his hands are numb, sir.  
Perhaps he’s only hiding where  
the river bends and hums, sir.

You loved him once—I heard you say,  
before your words grew rotten.  
You held us both above your head.  
You haven’t quite forgotten.

Don’t strike me. I am telling true.  
His footprints end together.  
The river took the smaller ones  
and carried on forever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem about a boy leaving a note for Jimmy Leonard after discovering Minnegan among the mud, roots, and garbage.
counterfactuals.output:
He found Minnegan where the river  
forgot what it had carried—  
half in mud, half under roots,  
among bottles, wire,  
and the soft rot of nameless things.

The boy did not call out.

Even the crows seemed careful  
with their black wings.  
Even the water moved around him  
as if ashamed.

He went home by the back lots,  
his shoes heavy with the bank,  
his hands smelling of iron  
and broken leaves.

For Jimmy Leonard  
he left a note beneath the door:

**I found him.  
Down past the leaning willow,  
where the garbage catches.  
Come before the rain.  
Come alone.**

Then he folded the evening  
around himself  
and waited—

a boy no longer certain  
that the earth kept secrets,  
only that it held them  
until someone came looking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
